meldungen.titel: Six state treasurers urge Anthropic to explain its AI risks before the listing, and suggest a delay if it cannot
meldungen.text:
On the eve of its Nasdaq debut, Anthropic has received a pointed letter from precisely the people whose pension money could soon flow into its shares. Six state financial officers have written to Dario Amodei, the chief executive, and the board of the Claude maker, asking the company to answer three questions publicly before its initial public offering: how it will manage the safety risks of its AI, why public shareholders will have so little say, and what would happen to the business if safety concerns slowed development. "If these concerns cannot be adequately addressed within the proposed timetable, delaying the offering would be appropriate," they write.

Their starting point is Anthropic's own prospectus, which acknowledges "risks that public markets have never before had to price". Among them is the prospect that ever more capable systems behave unpredictably or advance faster than humans can oversee them; the filing even concedes that a catastrophic AI incident could cause harm on a scale the insurance industry as a whole might be unable to cover. Disclosure alone, the officials argue, is therefore not enough. Investors need to understand how a serious safety incident, a suspended model deployment, new regulation or large liability claims would affect operations, contracts, liquidity and access to capital. It is also unclear who would decide on an emergency pause: the board, the Long-Term Benefit Trust or an independent safety body.

The second complaint concerns power. Under the prospectus, the trust elects four of the seven directors, while the seven co-founders together command 50.1 per cent of the vote despite owning only about 10 per cent of the fully diluted equity. Between them, trust and founders can fill the entire board, leaving outside shareholders with "essentially no say". The officials accept that the structure is meant to shield the safety mission from short-term commercial pressure, but they want a time-based sunset on the founders' voting rights, genuine shareholder participation in director elections and far more transparency about how the trust works.

The third point targets a tension at the heart of the business model. In his essay "We Must Pace the Frontier", Mr Amodei himself argued that frontier development may need to slow so that safety can keep up, yet the prospectus ties Anthropic's growth to staying ahead of rivals with the most advanced models, on top of computing commitments of roughly 900 billion dollars, much of it locked in by contract. The letter therefore asks for sensitivity analyses of six, 12 and 24 month delays, showing the effect on revenue, cash flow, debt service and profitability, and separating spending that could be deferred from obligations Anthropic would have to honour regardless.

The signatories, all Democrats, are Maryland's comptroller Brooke Lierman and the treasurers of Illinois, Connecticut, Colorado, New Mexico and Vermont. They stress that they write as elected officials, not on behalf of their pension funds, but note that index inclusion would push the stock automatically into retirement savings. It is not the first such intervention: in October New York City's comptroller, Mark Levine, who oversees more than 325 billion dollars of pension assets, urged a pause, and unions and a "Block the IPO" campaign have warned against an overvalued listing. With pricing due tonight, a delay looks improbable; the letter is more likely to shape the questions Anthropic faces as a listed company.

meldungen.titel: Cisco wires Claude Mythos 5 into its AI Defense platform, letting a select group of customers turn Anthropic's most guarded model on their own AI agents
meldungen.text:
Anthropic's most closely held model is getting a second outlet, under tight supervision. Cisco announced on Wednesday that it is building Claude Mythos 5 into AI Defense, its security platform for artificial intelligence applications, where the model will run what Cisco calls adaptive red teaming: attacking a company's own AI apps and agents to find weaknesses before somebody else does.

The choice of model is no accident. The Mythos line is regarded as unusually good at finding and exploiting security holes, which is precisely why Anthropic has kept it on a short leash. Its predecessor, Claude Mythos Preview, was released only to a handful of firms under Project Glasswing, with the aim of closing zero-day vulnerabilities proactively; those partners later received Mythos 5 as an upgrade. Cisco's integration packages the capability inside a commercial product for a broader set of customers.

Cisco's argument is that conventional red teaming cannot adequately test the risks peculiar to today's AI applications. Standardised checks probe for familiar problems such as prompt injection or the leakage of sensitive data. The adaptive approach instead analyses the target environment and devises attacks tailored to it: Mythos uses its extended reasoning to generate attack ideas, write concrete test payloads and adjust its tactics according to how the target system responds, much as a human penetration tester would.

The guard rails are extensive. Tests are confined to targets that have been registered and authorised in advance, and to test briefs defined by the customer. Every action is attributed to a named user and logged for audit, and the model cannot reach the public internet beyond the authorised test environment. Customers get controlled access to Mythos through AI Defense, not unrestricted use of its programming interface.

AI Defense's existing standard and adaptive red-teaming functions are already available. The Mythos extension will initially go to selected enterprise customers, with a wider rollout planned for approved clients; Cisco has not said which customer groups qualify.

The timing is telling. On the eve of its Nasdaq debut, Anthropic is showing investors that even a model it deems too dangerous for general release can earn money through a partner that takes on the job of policing its use.

meldungen.titel: Nvidia's first quarter without Jensen Huang smashes forecasts, but the fine print shows it is now bankrolling its own customers
meldungen.text:
Whatever turmoil engulfs its boardroom, Nvidia's order book appears untroubled. In the third quarter of its 2027 fiscal year the chipmaker booked revenue of 115.8 billion dollars, up 103 per cent on a year earlier and 20 per cent on the previous quarter. Wall Street had pencilled in about 109 billion, Nvidia itself 108 billion. Data centre sales rose 110 per cent to 107.6 billion dollars, edge computing (gaming PCs and devices) 42 per cent to 8.2 billion, and net income doubled to a record 65.3 billion. For the current quarter the company guides to 130 billion dollars, plus or minus 3 per cent, against analyst expectations of 125.2 billion. Shares, which had closed at 155.46 dollars, rose about 2 per cent after hours.

Colette Kress, interim chief executive and finance chief, presented the figures without mentioning her predecessor. "Our momentum is real," she said, describing the Vera Rubin generation as "off to an explosive start" and the fastest architecture ramp in the company's history, although the launch will squeeze gross margin to 71 to 72 per cent this quarter. Board chairman Harvey Jones opened the call by stating that the board "does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO" and would take no questions on his departure.

The more revealing passage sits in the CFO commentary rather than the press release. "Many are growing faster than their balance sheets and long-term credit profiles can support," Nvidia writes of the neoclouds and frontier labs that buy its chips. Its response is to step in: Nvidia is now liable for up to 118 billion dollars in guarantees, 105 billion of it for SB Energy's campus in Ohio, which is to host about 4.25 gigawatts of Nvidia hardware exclusively for OpenAI on 20 year leases. On top come up to 32 billion dollars of capacity agreements with neoclouds, while total future commitments, mostly multiyear memory purchases, have reached 518 billion dollars, 222 billion of it due within the coming fiscal year. Customers are also taking longer to pay: 64 days on average, up from 60, partly because of extended terms for some large buyers. Nvidia says it has not yet had to pay out on any guarantee.

Critics call this circular financing: Nvidia lends credibility and cash, and the money returns as chip orders. JPMorgan's Michael Cembalest notes that its commitments nearly doubled in a single quarter; investor Dan Niles expects Kress to rein them in, which would hurt neoclouds such as CoreWeave. China remains a blank in the outlook, and Nvidia will no longer sell to customers who rent more than half their GPUs to Chinese firms. Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon had already halved his price target to 200 dollars before the results.

Update: the boardroom saga is not over. On Tuesday Huang wrote on X that he would return as chief executive if the board wished, conceding that he had made "serious mistakes" in his private life and had fallen short of the standards Nvidia expects of everyone; he did not address suspicions that his affair with Alice Huang of Megaspeed may have helped circumvent US sanctions. Chairman Harvey Jones insists the resignation was accepted unanimously, yet Semafor, citing anonymous sources, reports that one faction of the board is working to bring him back. The board has meanwhile set up an oversight committee for national security, export controls and trade risk that reports to it and to Kress. Shares briefly rose about 5 per cent after hours.

meldungen.titel: Anthropic heads for Nasdaq with five share classes, and its founders keep the final say no matter how many shares they sell
meldungen.text:
Anthropic's flotation, with trading under the ticker ANT expected this week, will offer investors a slice of the profits but almost none of the power. The company is a public benefit corporation, committed to "the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity", and it has engineered a governance structure that neither a takeover bidder nor a majority of public shareholders can override. IBTimes reports an indicative price range of 70 to 78 dollars per share, subject to the final pricing.

According to Morningstar's analysis of the filing, control rests with two groups that hold little or no economic stake. The Long-Term Benefit Trust, five independent trustees with no equity and no share of profits, holds a single Class T share that lets it elect, and remove without cause, four of the seven directors. The seven co-founders, bundled in a "Founder LLC", hold a single Class F share that appoints the remaining directors and carries a fixed 50.1 per cent of the vote on every general matter. Inside the LLC each founder has one vote, so four of the seven can in effect decide any shareholder vote. Crucially, that 50.1 per cent does not shrink when the founders sell; reports say they could dispose of up to 98 per cent of their IPO-era holdings and keep the voting share.

Three further classes complete the picture. Class A, sold in the IPO and also held by early investors and staff, carries one vote per share but can never exceed 49.9 per cent of the total. Class N rewards strategic partners, chiefly Amazon and Alphabet, with profits but no votes; these shares convert into Class A when sold to unaffiliated buyers. Class E, to be issued to non-founder employees after the listing, gives staff a voice in one trust-elected board seat.

The design resembles Palantir's founder arrangement and is more rigid than Meta's dual-class model. Critics argue it leaves public shareholders with little accountability, and Morningstar notes it exempts Anthropic from some Nasdaq rules while limiting eligibility for certain major indices, which could dampen passive demand.

Update: the offering price is due to be set later today, with trading on Nasdaq starting on Thursday. Of the 825 million shares on offer, about 801 million are newly issued, so nearly all the proceeds go to the company; the seven co-founders sell the remaining 23.6 million, roughly 250 million dollars each according to The Wall Street Journal, and each keeps about 240 million shares. On the prospectus figures Amazon would own about 14.7 per cent afterwards and Alphabet about 13.7 per cent, and 5 per cent of the shares go to a dedicated public benefit fund. One awkward detail for you: the European prospectus, approved by BaFin, was not passported to Austria, as the Finanzmarktaufsicht (FMA, Austria's financial regulator) confirmed, so Austrian investors cannot subscribe and can only buy on the open market from Thursday. Unsolicited offers of "pre-listing" shares by email or messenger are not genuine. Demand looks strong: according to CNBC, cited by Reuters, Anthropic is considering enlarging the offering hours before pricing; at the current terms it would raise up to 64.4 billion dollars at a valuation of about one trillion, the second largest IPO in history after SpaceX (75 billion dollars in June).

meldungen.titel: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra takes second place behind Claude Fable 5.2, competing on price rather than brilliance
meldungen.text:
OpenAI has released two new models: GPT-6.2 Astra, its frontier model for the hardest work, and GPT-6.2 Sol, a leaner model for everyday tasks. Both are available to paying users of ChatGPT Work and Codex and via the API. On the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Astra lands second, three points behind Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2, and ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 at their highest effort settings.

The real argument is cost. A task in the index costs about 4 dollars with Astra at maximum reasoning, against up to 27 dollars for Fable 5.2, and OpenAI models now occupy most of the price performance frontier. Astra's token prices fall 20 per cent to 8 dollars per million input and 40 dollars per million output tokens. Sol matches the older GPT-6 Astra at roughly 15 per cent of the cost. Astra leads on 3D generation and robotics planning and on a science workflow benchmark, while Fable 5.2 stays ahead on factual knowledge and hard reasoning tests. In coding, Astra is flat and Sol slipped three points because it more often omits key facts.

OpenAI also struck a sober note: Astra is its first released model to reach the "High" threshold for AI self-improvement under its Preparedness Framework, and both models hit the top "Critical" level for cyber capabilities, so they ship with tighter safeguards. Developer reception has been rough. Theo Browne, the well known developer and YouTuber, wrote that he would not pick Astra over Claude Opus 5.5, citing endless loops and pointless questions; on one long task the model stopped after two hours to ask about internal file names.

meldungen.titel: ChatGPT Wallet: OpenAI lets its agents pay for you, without ever seeing your card
meldungen.text:
OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet on 13 November, the missing piece for its "dots" agents, which can now complete purchases on a user's behalf rather than merely filling a basket. You add a card once; thereafter each purchase needs only your approval, with no need to type in payment details again.

The design rests on tokenisation: the agent works with a substitute token for your American Express, Mastercard or Visa card and never sees the real number. The wallet holds neither a cash balance nor crypto. Responsibility stays where it was: merchants remain liable for delivery and returns, and billing disputes generally go through the card issuer, according to OpenAI's terms as reported by Decrypt.

For now the circle is small. The feature is open only to ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the United States, aged 18 or over and holding an eligible US-issued card; OpenAI reportedly wants to learn from real use before widening access. On the merchant side, a newly published Commerce Partner Playbook advises shops to let signed ChatGPT agent requests through their firewalls and to coordinate with payment and fraud providers, since risk systems may still reject perfectly legitimate agent purchases. The launch was no surprise: RuntimeWire had spotted the feature in the code of the Windows app beforehand.

The broader significance is that agentic shopping is moving from demonstration to infrastructure, with card networks, merchants and AI providers now negotiating who carries the risk when software, rather than a person, presses "buy".

meldungen.titel: Gemini Notebook can now turn your notes and sources into an interactive website with a quiz
meldungen.text:
Google's research tool, formerly NotebookLM and renamed Gemini Notebook a few months ago, has gained a feature that converts everything in a notebook, notes and sources alike, into an interactive web page. A prompt as simple as "build me a website" produces a first draft, but Google advises spelling out what the page should achieve if you want something genuinely useful.

Its showcase is telling: a student feeds in chemistry notes, asks for a page built around the periodic table and requests a quiz at the end to test what has been learnt. Google pitches the feature at students preparing for exams, but also at analysts visualising data such as sales reports and at teams who want an interactive project tracker. Finished pages can be shared with other users.

The feature is rolling out globally now to all users over 18, including those on Google Workspace subscriptions. For the moment it works only on the web; the mobile app is due to follow later.

meldungen.titel: "Ask Maps" arrives in Austria: Google Maps now answers questions instead of just searching for places
meldungen.text:
Google has launched "Ask Maps", first unveiled in March, in Austria, Germany and Switzerland. Next to the familiar search bar a blue "Ask" button with a magnifying glass appears; you can type or speak a question, and a multistage AI agent system gathers real-time data, including weather and traffic, to answer it.

Google's examples range from the practical to the ambitious: which restaurant on your saved brunch list has a table for six in 30 minutes, the most scenic route for a three hour motorbike ride, or live information about current congestion. How Google knows whether a restaurant still has free tables is not entirely clear. In the United States the feature can even order food for collection on your way home, through partners such as Square and Toast; Google told futurezone this is "not yet" available here.

The rollout is gradual. In a quick check, futurezone could not find the feature in the iOS or Android apps or in the browser version on launch day, and Google says it will appear soon.

meldungen.titel: Consulting Deep Dive, part 3: BCG, the most tech-heavy of the three MBB firms, and where its alumni go
meldungen.text:
Boston Consulting Group is one of the three "MBB" firms, alongside McKinsey and Bain. In 2025 it reported revenue of 14.4 billion dollars, its 22nd consecutive year of growth, and a workforce of 33,500 across more than 100 cities in over 50 countries. The single most important fact for anyone weighing BCG today: tech and AI focused services now account for more than 40 per cent of its revenue, a far larger share than the firm's classic strategy image suggests.

That shift is institutionalised in two units. BCG X, with more than 3,000 technologists, builders and designers, designs, builds and implements new solutions and businesses, typically involving AI; its specialisations are AI and software, design and digital growth, and it hires data scientists, engineers, product managers and "venture architects" alongside consultants. BCG Platinion is the technology strategy and implementation arm, recruiting consultants who understand how technology works in a business context. Generalist consultants, meanwhile, sit in industry practices such as industrial goods and in functional practices, and follow the familiar up-or-out ladder from associate or consultant to project leader, principal and partner.

Exits are, by most accounts, nearly identical to McKinsey's and Bain's. An analysis of more than 1,600 MBB departures cited by former Bain manager Taylor Warfield finds that about 31 per cent move into corporate or individual contributor roles, 14 per cent into financial services and 13 per cent into software and technology. Poets and Quants found that 62.8 per cent of MBB leavers join private companies, often venture or private equity backed, against 18.7 per cent who go to listed firms. Average tenure at top firms is roughly 2.7 years, so leaving after two to four years is the norm rather than a failure.

Corporate strategy is the most common destination, at manager to director level and, in US figures, 150,000 to 250,000 dollars in total pay. Private equity is the most coveted, with associates typically earning 250,000 to 350,000 dollars in the US; Bain's private equity practice is the classic feeder, but BCG alumni are said to be well placed at growth-oriented funds. BCG's tech weighting makes the move into big tech strategy, operations, product or chief of staff roles an easy story to tell, and startups usually recruit BCG alumni after two to five years as chief of staff or head of strategy. Venture capital remains a smaller, harder path.

What the sources do not provide is a school-by-school breakdown of BCG's European intake; for HEC, HSG, INSEAD, LBS, WHU and Nova, the schools' own employment reports are the reliable place to check, and part 16 of this series will compare them.

meldungen.titel: Oliver Wyman promotes 55 new partners for 2027, a markedly larger class than in recent years
meldungen.text:
Oliver Wyman, the strategy consultancy owned by Marsh McLennan, has named 55 new partners and two executive directors, who take office on 1 January 2027. The promotions span its network from Dubai to New York, according to the firm's announcement as reported by StreetInsider and Stock Titan.

The number matters chiefly by comparison. For 2026 the firm elected 40 partners and four executive directors, and for 2025 a combined 45 partners and executive directors. A class of 57 is therefore a clear step up. A larger partner intake usually signals confidence in future demand, and Oliver Wyman's core territory of financial services, risk and insurance is precisely where its owner gives it privileged access to clients.

meldungen.titel: McKinsey teams up with Cognition to sell AI software engineering to large companies
meldungen.text:
McKinsey and Cognition, the maker of the autonomous coding agent Devin, have formed an alliance to sell AI-driven software engineering to large companies in the United States and Europe. The division of labour is clear: McKinsey helps clients choose the engineering projects that matter most, sets a baseline for cost, speed and quality, and redesigns teams and workflows around AI; Cognition supplies Devin, which takes on engineering tasks and returns them for human review.

The firms justify the push with a McKinsey survey of 334 product and engineering leaders from the second quarter of 2026. In the top quarter of organisations, AI more than doubled productivity; at 30 per cent of them, productivity actually fell. Lari Hämäläinen, a senior partner in McKinsey's technology, media and telecoms practice, told Business Insider that until late 2025 most AI coding tools handled only narrow tasks, and that "it's a completely different thing to scale it across 2,000 developers or 20,000 developers." McKinsey says it has already helped more than 50 companies redesign software development around AI.

Cognition says Devin routes each kind of work to a different AI model, delivering frontier-level results for 60 per cent less ("You don't need to drive a Ferrari to the grocery store," says partnerships chief Art Levy). It counts six of the eight global systemically important banks among its clients, and the Polish software group Comarch is using it to rebuild its 20 year old ERP XL system within 18 months. Cognition was valued at 48 billion dollars in its last round and has reportedly discussed raising money at up to 80 billion. McKinsey has a similar arrangement with Cursor.

meldungen.titel: More dream sleep, fewer diseases: a 95,000-person study links REM sleep to lower risk of 83 conditions
meldungen.text:
How much you sleep matters, but so does how you sleep. A study published in PLOS Medicine by researchers led from Capital Medical University in Beijing analysed 95,559 participants of the UK Biobank, who wore wrist trackers for a week between 2013 and 2015. Their sleep patterns were then matched against hospital diagnoses for more than a thousand conditions over a median follow-up of almost nine years.

One sleep stage stood out. A greater amount of REM sleep, the phase in which most dreaming happens and brain activity resembles wakefulness, was associated with a lower risk of 83 diseases, among them heart failure, Alzheimer's disease, low blood pressure and atrial fibrillation. More deep sleep was linked to a lower risk of seven conditions, including type 2 diabetes and Parkinson's disease, and, according to German reports, severe depression. Irregular sleep and more time awake after falling asleep were tied to higher risks of three and six diseases respectively; large night-to-night swings in sleep duration were linked to a 26 per cent higher risk of severe depression.

Duration still counts. Six to eight hours emerged as a sweet spot: for 69 of the 86 conditions where length mattered, risk was lowest in that range, while sleeping under five hours was linked to a higher risk of 37 diseases. The REM effect held when the researchers looked at its proportion of total sleep, suggesting it is not simply a by-product of sleeping longer.

The caveats are real. The study shows associations, not causes; the trackers' sleep stage estimates agreed only moderately with laboratory measurements; and emerging illness may itself disturb sleep years before diagnosis. REM sleep depends mainly on total sleep time and on how continuous that sleep is, and is eroded by stress, alcohol and going against your body clock.

meldungen.titel: Vienna's Allocator One closes its first fund of funds above 100 million dollars, 23 per cent oversubscribed, and claims indirect stakes in 17 unicorns
meldungen.text:
Vienna has acquired a sizeable new gatekeeper for venture money. Allocator One, a fund of funds based in the Austrian capital, announced the final close of its first anchor vehicle, Flagship Fund I, which took place in September. The fund was 23 per cent oversubscribed and ended with commitments of more than 100 million US dollars from family offices, successful tech founders, seasoned venture investors and institutions in more than 25 countries. It invests in funds of the 2023 to 2026 vintages.

Its niche is the "emerging manager": venture firms raising their first or second fund. Since starting in July 2024, Allocator One says it has backed more than 40 such funds, most recently Noctua Science Ventures, with tickets of two to ten million dollars. In over 60 per cent of them it is the largest investor. Through those funds it is indirectly exposed to some 600 companies, among them 17 unicorns including Lovable, Thinking Machines and xAI, and it has already returned 11 per cent of paid-in capital.

The founding partners, Michael Ströck and Felix Staeritz, present manager selection as a data exercise. Roughly 1,000 new emerging-manager funds are launched worldwide each year; Allocator One estimates it screens about 80 per cent of them, invites just under a fifth to interview and, after due diligence, backs the top one per cent. The process combines human judgement with its own fund infrastructure platform, Infra One, and an AI agent called Ori. Finding exceptional managers, Ströck says, "should not depend on whose pitch happens to reach you".

The figures are self-reported and the fund is young, so the real test, distributions from the underlying portfolios over the next decade, lies ahead. Still, a 100-million-dollar fund of funds run from Vienna is a rarity in a market where emerging managers usually raise from American or pan-European allocators.

meldungen.titel: Brussels hands Vienna's Prewave its first Apply AI Startup Award, a year after its own red-tape cuts forced the supply-chain specialist to shed staff
meldungen.text:
The European Commission has named Prewave, a Viennese scale-up that uses AI to monitor supply chains, one of three winners of its inaugural Apply AI Startup Award. The prize, run by the European AI Office with the EU project AI-BOOST, honours the most innovative AI start-ups in strategic sectors such as health, manufacturing, energy and the public sector. Henna Virkkunen, the Commission's executive vice-president for technological sovereignty, presented the trophy on Tuesday at the Apply AI Summit in Brussels.

National start-up associations had nominated 24 companies from 16 member states over the summer; ten reached the final, among them the Slovak dental start-up AI Dental, which recently moved its growth base to Vienna. After online pitches in October the jury picked Prewave. There is no cash attached, only a trophy, a certificate and a slot on the summit's main stage. Co-founder Lisa Smith, who now runs the company's public-sector business, accepted it, arguing that supply chains "have long been a question of sovereignty and resilience too".

Founded in 2017 as a spin-off from TU Wien by Smith and Harald Nitschinger, now sole chief executive, Prewave scans data across more than 200 risk categories in over 400 languages to warn companies early of supplier disruption, from strikes and natural disasters to human-rights abuses. More than 250 firms use it, including Lufthansa, Ferrari and Toyota, and it says it is the only Europe-headquartered vendor rated a Leader in Gartner's Magic Quadrant for supply-chain risk management. It has raised more than 90 million euros; Volvo and the family office of Rolex's founder invested last year.

The irony is hard to miss. In summer 2025 Prewave cut 20 jobs, about 8 per cent of staff, after the EU's Omnibus package diluted the supply-chain due-diligence directive whose obligations its software helps companies meet. Its pitch has since shifted from compliance to sovereignty and resilience, in a market crowded with American rivals such as Resilinc, Interos and Everstream Analytics and with Mannheim's Osapiens, now a unicorn.

meldungen.titel: Uber and China's Momenta start a robotaxi pilot in Munich, in BMW's own backyard
meldungen.text:
Chinese software has taken the wheel in BMW's home city. Uber and Momenta, a Beijing-based specialist in autonomous driving, have launched a robotaxi pilot in Munich. Anyone interested can join a waiting list in the Uber app, with access granted in phases, and a trained safety operator rides along on every trip.

The cars cover a defined zone across much of northern Munich, including the neighbourhoods around the Olympic Park, with more districts to follow. Approved riders who book UberX, Electric or Comfort inside the zone may be offered an autonomous car; pick-ups and drop-offs are limited to designated stops. Rides are free because the test permit does not allow commercial service, and neither company will say how many vehicles are on the road or when a paid service might start. The legal basis is a permit from the Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (Germany's federal motor transport authority), granted to Momenta in July, which lets it test Level 4 automated driving in urban traffic nationwide. Germany's strict regime, says Momenta's robotaxi chief Shuo Xie, "has set one of the global benchmarks for autonomous driving".

Momenta, founded in 2016, already runs its own robotaxi fleet in China but is better known as a supplier: BMW and Mercedes-Benz use its driver assistance systems in cars built for the Chinese market. For Uber, which sold its own self-driving unit in 2020, the deal fits a platform strategy of hosting other companies' robotaxis; its European partners now include Momenta, the British start-up Wayve and China's Pony.ai.

Europe still has no service that is both driverless and commercial. Zagreb has come closest: the Croatian start-up Verne runs paid rides with Pony.ai technology, still with a safety operator, and has been testing fully driverless trips to the airport since September with about 30 vehicles. Uber and Wayve have operated in London since September with fewer than 20 cars, Waymo awaits approval there, and Volkswagen's MOIA is testing autonomous ID. Buzz vans in Hamburg.

The politics are less settled. The United States has largely barred Chinese software for connected and autonomous vehicles from the 2027 model year, citing espionage and data security; the EU has no such rule. The announcement does not say where data from the Munich pilot will be processed and stored.

meldungen.titel: Exit in Vienna: SPG buys loss-making cloud specialist ORBIT four years after its founding
meldungen.text:
The Viennese IT services group SPG (Specific-Group) is acquiring 100 per cent of ORBIT Cloud Solutions, a cloud specialist founded in Vienna in 2022. The price was not disclosed. The brand survives as "ORBIT Cloud Solutions, powered by SPG", and managing director Lanna O'Reilly and director of operations Gregor Nussbaumer stay on, so clients keep their contacts.

ORBIT steers companies in regulated industries, mostly banks and insurers, from cloud strategy through migration to daily operations, and advises on security and compliance under the EU's DORA, NIS2 and AI Act. It is built around Microsoft Azure, where it holds six Microsoft specialisations, but also works with AWS, Google Cloud and Oracle. It has not yet turned a profit: the 2025 accounts show an accumulated deficit of about 1.55 million euros, implying a loss of roughly 355,000 euros for 2025 alone.

SPG, owner-managed since 1998 and based on Hoher Markt, modernises the legacy core systems of banks, insurers, utilities and the public sector, and says it employs more than 500 people from over ten countries. Its holding, whose shareholders include managing directors Marcus Brandstetter and Andreas Muzik as well as CCA Invest, also owns several other IT firms and 60 per cent of Dormy. Muzik calls the deal a targeted expansion, with cloud, security and software increasingly sold by one provider.

The logic is regulatory: since DORA took effect, banks must police their IT and cloud suppliers far more closely, and NIS2 widens cyber duties to many more sectors. In that market a small team competes with Accenture, Kapsch BusinessCom, ACP, Bechtle and Cloudflight, which makes the backing of a 500-strong group a selling point.

meldungen.titel: Europe's second-best venture year ever, and America still invested five times more in AI in nine months than Europe did in a decade
meldungen.text:
European technology is enjoying a bumper year that looks rather less triumphant on closer inspection. Atomico's State of European Tech 2026, the London venture firm's annual report built on Dealroom data and surveys of founders, investors and policymakers, projects that European start-ups will raise about 81 billion dollars this year. That is 62 per cent more than the 50 billion of 2025 and only just short of the 2021 record of 94 billion. A record 58 European companies became unicorns in the first nine months, against 42 in the whole of last year, and the ecosystem is now valued at 4.4 trillion dollars, up from 0.9 trillion in 2017.

The money, however, is flowing to ever fewer hands. First rounds (pre-seed and seed) fell 28 per cent between 2021 and 2025 and are projected to fall again. Even at seed stage, 43 per cent of capital went into just five rounds, among them Ineffable Intelligence at 1.1 billion dollars; at Series A the share was 55 per cent, led by Isomorphic Labs at 2.1 billion. "It feels like we are heading straight into a bubble," warns Sara Rywe of ByFounders. Funds are not keeping pace: the median European fund is 70 million dollars, 29 per cent below its 2024 peak, and no European fund has raised more than a billion this year.

The comparison abroad is sobering. China overtook Europe in venture investment this year, and in AI drew 35 billion dollars against Europe's 20 billion. American compute and AI companies took 284 billion; the US increase alone exceeded everything Europe has put into AI over ten years, and OpenAI and Anthropic absorbed 61 per cent of global funding. Europe's share of global venture capital has slid from 20 per cent in 2022 to about 9.4 per cent. Its net inflow of tech talent has shrunk from about 72,000 in 2022 to roughly 11,000.

Founding, meanwhile, is booming: some 40,000 people started a tech company in Europe this year, up 36 per cent, more than 60 per cent of them alone, a shift Atomico credits to AI lowering the cost of building products. Europe now hosts 29 per cent of the world's new tech founders, and 29 per cent of surveyed tech managers want to found a company next. The catch is plain: a record crop of founders chasing a shrinking pool of early money.

Update: the Austrian figures in the report are unflattering. Austrian start-ups are on course for about 465 million dollars this year, more than double 2025, yet that is only 0.08 per cent of GDP, level with Norway and ahead of only Italy and Poland among the top 20 (Sweden: 0.78 per cent, Germany: 0.24 per cent). Pension funds in the DACH region put just 0.001 per cent of their assets into venture capital, and Austria's planned fund of funds is not expected before 2027.

meldungen.titel: Vienna's Stackreps turns lecture notes into an AI study plan, backed by 200,000 euros of Microsoft cloud credits
meldungen.text:
"Most people learn inefficiently because they have no real strategy and read things a hundred times," says David Fingerlos, co-founder of the Viennese startup Stackreps. His answer is a platform that combines large language models with two well researched learning techniques: spaced repetition, in which material is revisited at set intervals, and active recall, in which knowledge is deliberately retrieved from memory.

Users upload their material as PDFs, slide decks or e-books. Stackreps produces summaries, multiple choice tests, digital flashcards and an AI-generated study podcast in which two voices discuss the content, interspersed with revision questions. The user enters an exam date, and the platform builds a schedule and adjusts repetition intervals so that knowledge peaks on the day. Fingerlos, a computer scientist specialising in data science, founded the company in 2024 with Sebastian Güngöze and Eric Lipp, both originally from law, who taught themselves programming and machine learning.

Technically, Stackreps draws on existing models from OpenAI and Mistral, which it says run only on European servers, with an in-house processing layer that structures information for the models and several checking steps to reduce errors. Early development was funded partly by a pre-seed grant from Austria Wirtschaftsservice (aws). Through TechNvst and the Microsoft Investor Network, the startup now receives cloud and AI infrastructure worth 200,000 euros over two years, allowing it to run on Azure without bearing the cost. It is not yet profitable, admits that marketing is "a blind spot", and plans partnerships with universities and international expansion.

meldungen.titel: The ECB warns that the AI share boom echoes the dotcom peak, on the eve of Anthropic's listing
meldungen.text:
The European Central Bank publishes its twice-yearly Financial Stability Review today, and its message has been trailed with unusual bluntness. Vice-President Boris Vujčić, previewing the report on Monday, said the "rapid expansion of AI is creating new challenges for financial stability" and that a reassessment of the AI narrative could trigger an abrupt repricing and significant valuation losses.

His central comparison is historical. Money raised through new stock market listings, measured against the size of the US economy, is on course to exceed the peak of the late-1990s dotcom boom, and such surges, he noted, have often coincided with market tops. The timing is pointed: Anthropic is expected to debut on Nasdaq on Thursday in what could be the second-largest listing ever, raising about 61 billion dollars at a valuation near 1.2 trillion. Large US technology firms are projected to spend 5.5 trillion dollars on capital investment by 2030, increasingly financed through record bond issuance.

Cracks are already visible. The Nasdaq sits nearly 8 per cent below its high after results from Alphabet, Intel and Amazon, and markets were further unsettled by Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia and by the US midterms, in which the Democrats won both chambers. Europe is not insulated: eurozone investment funds have loaded up on AI-linked assets, so a slump in US valuations would land squarely on European savers.

The ECB names two further risks: rising yields on the bonds of heavily indebted governments such as France, where it insists the remedy must be fiscal rather than central-bank intervention, and fast-growing, lightly monitored non-bank lenders. It wants redemption rules for funds to reflect how quickly they can sell assets, and leverage limits for hedge funds. All three risks, Vujčić warned, could strike at once; banks, by contrast, are well capitalised.

Update: the full report, published on Wednesday, goes further than the preview. In a box on how AI is financed, the ECB writes that the rapid shift towards debt "invokes historical parallels with the dotcom and subprime bubbles". The dotcom echo is overinvestment in infrastructure; the subprime echo is circular financing, off-balance-sheet deals and opaque private markets. Hyperscalers commit to renting data centres and chips owned by others, who then borrow against those future payments; economically that is debt, but under US accounting rules it does not appear on the tech giants' balance sheets. Using an AI agent built on OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol to comb through SEC filings, the ECB puts these hidden commitments at more than 4 trillion dollars, well above reported liabilities. It also flags a maturity mismatch (bonds outliving chips whose useful life the IMF puts at about two years) and notes that Alphabet's and Amazon's earnings are increasingly flattered by valuation gains on their Anthropic stakes.
